questions.key_step: \sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2} is 2\tan^{-1}x only on [-1,1]; it changes form for x>1 and x<-1, so solve interval by interval.
questions.justification: Branch of sin^-1(2x/(1+x^2)) for three intervals, casework with tan^-1 sum identities; extraneous roots. Short but needs correct branches; no insight beyond the standard identity.

questions.key_step: On both sides of 0 the denominator collapses to x^2, so the limit is the standard \frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}\to1.
questions.justification: Left and right limits with [x] and {x}; both denominators collapse to x^2. Routine one-sided evaluation; one idea applied twice.

questions.key_step: Differentiability needs continuity first (this fixes a+b and c), then equality of the one-sided slopes gives a-b.
questions.justification: Continuity gives a+b and c; one-sided derivatives with series give a-b; solve. Chain of routine steps (continuity, expansion, one-sided slopes), no insight.

questions.key_step: Each element is in exactly one of four regions (both, only A, only B, neither); the odd-size condition is handled by \frac{(p+q)^5-(p-q)^5}{2}.
questions.justification: Conditional probability over pairs of subsets; per-element 3 vs 2 regions; odd-sum binomial trick. Counting set-up with two conditions plus an odd-term binomial sum; options help check.

questions.key_step: A factor tending to 0 times a bounded oscillating factor gives continuity; the difference quotient decides differentiability.
questions.justification: Piecewise function with bounded oscillation: four statements each need a check, including lim f'. Four genuine checks (continuity, non-differentiability by oscillation, f'(-1), limit of f').

questions.key_step: At an integer k, \sin\pi x vanishes, which kills the jump of \lfloor x\rfloor, but the one-sided slopes still differ unless |x^2-4x+3|=0 there.
questions.justification: [x]|x^2-4x+3| sin(pi x): one-sided derivatives at every integer decide all four statements. Needs general one-sided derivatives at every integer k (not just one point) and the exceptional integers 1 and 3; one slip changes the set in (D).

questions.key_step: Total probability for P(W), then Bayes' theorem; a roll greater than 3 is exactly the event "bag B_3".
questions.justification: Total probability and Bayes with three bags; four routine conditional probabilities. Routine chain, no insight; four statements each a short computation.

questions.key_step: The mode 8 occurs 2 or 3 times among x_5,x_6,x_7 (with x_7>8 free when it occurs twice); for "can be / least / maximum" statements one valid data set is enough.
questions.justification: Data set with fixed mean, median, unique mode: casework on frequency of the mode and distinct lower values; the PDF itself missed cases. Precision-heavy casework with a tie trap and no way to check; statements ask for totals and extremes.

questions.key_step: Condition on N: P(X=0)=\sum_nP(N=n)\left(\frac45\right)^n, a geometric series.
questions.justification: Geometric N, binomial X given N; sum of a geometric series. Single formula chain (total probability + geometric series).

questions.key_step: A wins exactly when N is odd; evaluate P(X=2\text{ and }N\text{ odd}) with \sum_{k\ge1}\binom{2k+1}{2}t^k=\frac{t(3+t)}{(1-t)^3}.
questions.justification: Conditional probability that N is odd given X=2: needs P(X=2) and a negative-binomial type series for odd N. Long exact series computation with an uncommon identity; no cross-check, high precision risk.

questions.key_step: Count all paths, then subtract those through (1,1) or (2,2) by inclusion-exclusion.
questions.justification: Lattice paths avoiding two points by inclusion-exclusion. One familiar move (inclusion-exclusion with binomials).

questions.key_step: Decide each \max/\min by the sign of x and the numerator becomes 7x^3 on both sides.
questions.justification: Limit with max/min of multiples of x; evaluate sign-wise and use ln(1+x)~x. Routine multi-step evaluation, no real insight.

questions.key_step: The maximum of two functions has corners only where the graphs cross with different slopes (or where the dominant function has its own corner).
questions.justification: Count corners of max{|4/pi atan x|, |2x^2-1|} using the graph and crossings. Graph sketch with exact counting of crossings, no options to check; hidden kinks at 0 and 1/sqrt2 and an unobvious crossing near 0.47.

questions.key_step: The shortest distance between a curve and a circle lies along the common normal, which passes through the centre, so minimise PC.
questions.justification: Min distance from the centre (3,0) to the parabola by common normal. Standard idea (distance to centre) then a quartic or quadratic minimisation.

questions.key_step: Dividing by e^{x+y} makes g(t)=\frac{f(t)}{e^t} additive, so g(t)=kt and f(t)=kte^t.
questions.justification: Functional equation made additive by dividing by e^(x+y); tangent gives k; n-th derivative of 2te^t. Single standard trick plus a Leibniz pattern; chain of 3 stages.

questions.key_step: The median 23 lies in the class 20-30, so use the median formula with N=28+k and cumulative frequency 16 below the class.
questions.justification: Median formula for grouped data with unknown frequency. One formula applied once, then a linear equation.

questions.key_step: Count all non-consecutive 4-subsets, then subtract those with no multiple of 3; the leftover numbers fall into consecutive pairs plus one isolated number.
questions.justification: 4-subsets with no two consecutive and a multiple of 3: complement and grouping into consecutive pairs. Counting with a small trick (pairs plus isolated 10), precision risk without options.

questions.key_step: Recognise both sums as binomial expansions: A=(1+x+x^2)^{10} and B=(1-x)^{10}, whose product is (1-x^3)^{10}.
questions.justification: Recognise two sums as (1+x+x^2)^10 and (1-x)^10, product is (1-x^3)^10. Recognition of binomial sums, then one coefficient.
